chem_ocra.6.0.summary: Chemical reactions involve energy changes due to the breaking and making of chemical bonds. Exothermic reactions transfer thermal energy to the surroundings, causing temperature to increase, whereas endothermic reactions absorb thermal energy from the surroundings, causing temperature to drop. Understanding these energy transfers is vital for evaluating industrial processes, chemical hand warmers, and self-cooling cans.

core.h: Conservation of Energy in Chemical Reactions
core.p: During any chemical reaction, energy is conserved: it is neither created nor destroyed. The total energy of the universe remains constant, meaning any energy released or absorbed by the reacting chemicals must be balanced by an equal and opposite energy change in the surroundings.
bullets: Energy is conserved in all chemical processes.
The reacting chemicals and the glass container form the system.
Everything else outside the system constitutes the surroundings.
Energy is transferred between the system and the surroundings.

callouts.p: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred from one form to another.

core.p: An exothermic reaction is one that transfers thermal energy to the surroundings. As a result, the temperature of the surroundings increases, which can be measured using a thermometer placed in the reaction mixture.
bullets: Thermal energy is transferred from the chemical system to the surroundings.
Thermometer shows an increase in temperature.
The container feels warm or hot to the touch.
Examples include combustion, oxidation, and neutralization reactions.

callouts.p: Exothermic reactions heat up the surroundings.

core.p: An endothermic reaction is one that takes in thermal energy from the surroundings. This causes the temperature of the surroundings to decrease, which is observed as the thermometer reading falls.
bullets: Thermal energy is absorbed by the chemical system from the surroundings.
Thermometer shows a decrease in temperature.
The container feels cold to the touch.
Examples include thermal decomposition and the reaction between citric acid and sodium hydrogencarbonate.

callouts.p: Endothermic reactions cool down the surroundings.

core.p: Energy changes are fundamentally driven by chemical bonds. Breaking existing chemical bonds requires energy and is an endothermic process, while making new chemical bonds releases energy and is an exothermic process.
bullets: Bond breaking is always endothermic (absorbs energy).
Bond making is always exothermic (releases energy).
Overall energy change depends on the difference between energy required to break bonds and energy released making bonds.
If more energy is released than absorbed, the reaction is exothermic.

callouts.p: MEXO: Making EXOthermic. Breaking takes energy.

core.p: Combustion of fuels (such as methane burning in oxygen) releases vast amounts of thermal energy. Neutralization reactions between acids and alkalis are also consistently exothermic.
bullets: Combustion transfers heat to surroundings to warm homes or power engines.
Neutralisation of hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide increases solution temperature.
Respiration in living cells is an exothermic process maintaining body temperature.

callouts.p: Reaction between an acid and a base producing a salt and water, releasing heat.
Do not confuse dissolving with neutralisation; some dissolving processes are endothermic.

core.p: Thermal decomposition requires continuous heating to break down a compound into simpler substances. Because energy must be constantly supplied, the reaction is strongly endothermic.
bullets: Example: Copper carbonate decomposing into copper oxide and carbon dioxide upon heating.
CaCO3 decomposed into CaO and CO2 by heating.
If heating is removed, the reaction stops immediately.

callouts.p: Breaking down a substance using heat energy.

core.h: Required Practical: Temperature Changes in Reactions
core.p: You must be able to investigate how temperature changes affect different reactions, such as acid plus metal, acid plus carbonate, or neutralization between acid and alkali.
bullets: Use a polystyrene cup inside a glass beaker for insulation to reduce heat loss.
Measure initial temperatures of reactants before mixing.
Stir the mixture with a thermometer and record the maximum or minimum temperature reached.
Calculate temperature change by subtracting initial from final temperature.

callouts.p: Polystyrene cup and lid reduce thermal energy transfer to the room, improving accuracy.

core.p: To obtain reliable temperature change data, repeating experiments and calculating mean values is essential. Graphical analysis helps identify anomalies and find peak temperature changes.
bullets: Plot temperature against volume of reagent added.
Draw two lines of best fit and find their intersection point for maximum temperature change.
Discard anomalous results before calculating means.
Control variables such as starting temperature and concentration of solutions.

callouts.p: Real temperature changes are often lower than theoretical values due to heat escaping to the surroundings.

core.p: Exothermic reactions are applied in commercial products such as self-heating cans and hand warmers.
bullets: Hand warmers use crystallisation of supersaturated sodium ethanoate or oxidation of iron.
Self-heating coffee cans mix calcium oxide with water to release heat safely.
Provide portable thermal energy without external electricity.

callouts.p: Utilise exothermic oxidation or crystallisation processes.

core.p: Endothermic processes are utilised in instant cold packs used for treating sports injuries.
bullets: Instant cold packs contain ammonium nitrate and water separated by a fragile barrier.
Squeezing the pack breaks the barrier, allowing ammonium nitrate to dissolve endothermically.
Absorbs heat from the injured area, reducing swelling and pain rapidly.

callouts.p: Disposable device using an endothermic dissolution process to lower temperature.

core.p: Although reaction profiles are covered elsewhere, understanding how energy levels connect to temperature changes is crucial. In exothermic reactions, products have less energy than reactants.
bullets: Reactants start higher than products in exothermic reactions.
Difference represents thermal energy transferred to surroundings.
Products start lower than reactants in endothermic reactions.
Difference represents thermal energy absorbed from surroundings.

callouts.p: Exo = Down overall. Endo = Up overall.

core.h: Higher Tier: Bond Energy Calculations Context
core.p: At Higher tier, quantitative energy changes are calculated using bond energies. The overall energy change is the sum of energies needed to break bonds minus the sum of energies released when bonds form.
bullets: Energy change = Sum(Bonds broken) - Sum(Bonds made).
Negative value indicates exothermic reaction.
Positive value indicates endothermic reaction.
Units are typically kJ/mol.

callouts.p: Reactants minus Products for bond energy calculations.

analogy.t: The Credit Card Bank Account Analogy
analogy.p: Imagine breaking bonds as withdrawing money from an account (you must put in effort/energy to get cash out, which is endothermic), and making bonds as depositing money back into the account, which rewards you with extra spending cash (releasing energy, exothermic). The net balance change tells you if you gained or lost overall energy. However, this analogy breaks down because chemical bonds do not store money in a literal bank vault, and energy is purely transferred as thermal energy or light rather than physical currency.

terms.d: A reaction that transfers thermal energy to the surroundings, increasing the temperature.
A reaction that takes in thermal energy from the surroundings, decreasing the temperature.
Everything outside the reacting chemicals, including the container and the air.
The reacting chemicals themselves taking part in the chemical change.
The minimum amount of energy particles must have to react successfully.
Breaking down a substance using thermal energy.
Reaction between an acid and a base producing salt and water.
Reaction where a substance burns in oxygen, releasing heat.
Measuring thermal energy changes in chemical reactions.
The energy required to break one mole of a specific chemical bond.
Principle that energy cannot be created or destroyed.
An insulator used in calorimetry experiments to prevent heat loss.

mistakes.w: Writing that temperature goes down in an exothermic reaction because it feels hot.
mistakes.r: Temperature of the surroundings goes UP in an exothermic reaction; the container feels hot because heat is transferred TO your hand from the reaction.

mistakes.w: Stating that bond breaking releases energy.
mistakes.r: Bond breaking ALWAYS absorbs energy (endothermic). Energy is only released when bonds are MADE.

mistakes.w: Forgetting the insulating lid in the calorimetry practical.
mistakes.r: A lid is essential to minimize heat loss to the room, ensuring accurate temperature change readings.
Endothermic reactions absorb thermal energy from the surroundings, causing a temperature drop; cold is the absence of heat.

mistakes.w: Mixing up reactants and products energy levels in exothermic profiles.
mistakes.r: In exothermic profiles, reactants are higher than products because energy is released.
Combustion is always exothermic as it releases heat and light energy.

exam.q: Define an exothermic reaction in terms of energy and temperature.
model: A reaction that transfers thermal energy to the surroundings (1)
causing the temperature of the surroundings to increase (1)
exam.tip: Mention both energy transfer and temperature change for full marks.

exam.q: Explain why thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate is classified as endothermic.
model: Thermal energy is absorbed from the surroundings (1)
to break chemical bonds in calcium carbonate (1)
exam.tip: Link energy absorption specifically to bond breaking.

exam.q: Describe how you would carry out a required practical to measure the temperature change when neutralising hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide.
model: Measure set volume of acid into a polystyrene cup (1)
Record initial temperature using a thermometer (1)
Add measured volume of sodium hydroxide and stir (1)
Record the highest temperature reached (1)
Calculate temperature change by subtracting initial from final (1)
Repeat to calculate a mean (1)
exam.tip: Always include insulation (polystyrene cup) and repeat for reliability.

exam.q: Explain in terms of bond breaking and bond making why a reaction is exothermic overall.
model: Energy is absorbed to break bonds in reactants (1)
Energy is released when new bonds form in products (1)
More energy is released in bond making than is absorbed in bond breaking (1)
Overall energy change is negative / energy is transferred to surroundings (1)
exam.tip: Compare the relative amounts of energy absorbed and released.

exam.q: A student adds ammonium nitrate to water in a beaker. The temperature drops by 5 C. Name the type of reaction.
model: Endothermic (1)
exam.tip: Temperature drop always indicates an endothermic process.

exam.q: State why a polystyrene cup with a lid is used instead of a glass beaker in calorimetry experiments.
model: Polystyrene is a better insulator (1)
reducing heat loss to the surroundings / giving more accurate temperature readings (1)
exam.tip: Reference reduction of heat transfer to surroundings.

exam.q: Give two everyday applications of exothermic reactions.
model: Hand warmers (1)
Self-heating food cans (1)
exam.tip: Accept self-heating cans, hand warmers, or chemical burn gels.

exam.q: Explain why energy must be supplied to break chemical bonds.
model: Forces of attraction hold atoms together in bonds (1)
Energy is needed to overcome these attractive forces (1)
exam.tip: Focus on overcoming electrostatic forces.

exam.q: Describe the energy change shown on an energy profile for an endothermic reaction.
model: Products are at a higher energy level than reactants (1)
Energy is taken in from the surroundings (1)
exam.tip: Check reactant and product levels carefully.

worked.q: Calculate the overall energy change for the reaction: H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl, given bond energies (kJ/mol): H-H = 436, Cl-Cl = 242, H-Cl = 431.
steps: Identify bonds broken in reactants: 1 x (H-H) and 1 x (Cl-Cl).
Calculate energy required to break bonds: 436 + 242 = 678 kJ/mol.
Identify bonds made in products: 2 x (H-Cl).
Calculate energy released making bonds: 2 x 431 = 862 kJ/mol.
Subtract energy released from energy required: 678 - 862 = -184 kJ/mol.

worked.q: A student mixes 25 cm3 of dilute hydrochloric acid with 25 cm3 of sodium hydroxide solution. The initial temperature is 18.5 C and the highest temperature reached is 26.0 C. Calculate the temperature change.
steps: Identify initial temperature: 18.5 C.
Identify final maximum temperature: 26.0 C.
Subtract initial temperature from final temperature: 26.0 - 18.5.

worked.q: Explain whether photosynthesis is exothermic or endothermic.
steps: Recall the process of photosynthesis: plants take in light energy from the Sun.
Determine direction of energy transfer: energy is absorbed from the surroundings.
Conclude classification based on energy absorption.
worked.ans: Endothermic because light energy is absorbed from the surroundings.

chem_ocra.6.2.summary: Calculating energy changes from bond energies allows chemists to predict whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic without performing physical experiments. By comparing the energy required to break bonds in reactants with the energy released when new bonds form in products, we determine the overall enthalpy change of the reaction. This quantitative approach is fundamental for comparing fuel efficiencies and designing industrial chemical processes safely and efficiently.

core.p: Every chemical bond holds a specific amount of stored chemical potential energy. To break any chemical bond, energy must always be absorbed from the surroundings, making bond breaking an endothermic process. Conversely, when new chemical bonds are formed, energy is always released into the surroundings, making bond formation an exothermic process.
bullets: Bond breaking requires energy (endothermic, positive enthalpy change).
Bond formation releases energy (exothermic, negative enthalpy change).
Stronger bonds require more energy to break and release more energy when formed.
The overall energy change of a reaction depends on the net difference between energy absorbed and energy released.

callouts.p: The energy required to break one mole of a specific covalent bond in gaseous molecules, measured in kilojoules per mole (kJ/mol).
Students often think bond formation absorbs energy because it feels counterintuitive that making things releases energy. Always remember: making bonds forms stable states, releasing energy.

core.p: A chemical reaction is a two-stage process in terms of energy: first, existing bonds are broken, and second, new bonds are formed. If the energy put in to break bonds is greater than the energy released when making bonds, the reaction is overall endothermic. If more energy is released by forming bonds than was put in to break them, the reaction is overall exothermic.
bullets: Endothermic reactions: Energy absorbed (breaking) > Energy released (forming).
Exothermic reactions: Energy released (forming) > Energy absorbed (breaking).
Overall enthalpy change (delta H) is negative for exothermic and positive for endothermic reactions.
Bond energy values provided in exams are usually average bond energies calculated across various molecules.

callouts.p: Bond energies are averages because the exact energy to break a specific bond varies slightly depending on the rest of the molecule's structure.

core.h: The Master Equation for Enthalpy Change
core.p: To calculate the exact energy change (delta H) for any reaction using bond energies, you must apply a standard formula. You sum all the bond energies of the reactants to find the total energy needed to break them, and sum all the bond energies of the products to find the total energy released. Subtracting the total product energy from the total reactant energy gives the overall enthalpy change.
bullets: Formula: Delta H = Sum of bond energies of reactants - Sum of bond energies of products.
Alternative formulation: Delta H = Energy absorbed to break bonds - Energy released forming bonds.
Always multiply individual bond energies by the stoichiometric balancing number in the equation.
Check all units are consistent, typically given in kJ/mol.

callouts.p: Always write out displayed formulas for reactants and products before counting bonds to ensure you do not miss any double bonds, single bonds, or multiplier coefficients.

core.h: Step 1: Identifying and Counting Bonds in Reactants
core.p: Before calculating energy, you must accurately count every single covalent bond present in the reactant molecules based on balanced chemical equations. Drawing out full displayed formulas (showing every atom and covalent bond explicitly) is essential for avoiding counting errors.
bullets: Draw out all reactant molecules using lines for single (dash), double (double dash), and triple covalent bonds.
Count every individual bond type (e.g., C-H, O=O, C=C).
Multiply the bond count by the balancing coefficient of that molecule in the balanced equation.
Sum the bond energies for all reactant bonds to find total energy input.

callouts.p: A molecule of oxygen (O2) contains a double bond (O=O), not two single bonds. A molecule of carbon dioxide (CO2) contains two double bonds (O=C=O).

core.h: Step 2: Identifying and Counting Bonds in Products
core.p: Just as with reactants, you must draw and count every covalent bond in the product molecules. The energy released when these bonds form constitutes the second part of the calculation. Accuracy here is vital since a single missed bond will ruin the final subtraction.
bullets: Draw full displayed formulas for all products.
Count each specific bond type present across all product molecules.
Multiply by any large stoichiometric numbers in front of the product formulas.
Sum all product bond energies to find total energy released.

callouts.p: Water (H2O) contains two O-H single bonds per molecule. If a reaction produces 2H2O, you have 4 O-H bonds in total to calculate.

core.p: Once you have listed the bonds and their individual bond energy values from the data table, multiply the quantity of each bond by its energy value. Add all these individual bond energy products together to get the total energy required to break all reactant bonds.
bullets: Create a clear tally table of bond type, number of bonds, bond energy, and subtotal.
Sum all subtotals to get total energy to break bonds (Reactants).
Ensure values correspond directly to the provided exam data table, never memorize bond energy numbers.
Double-check arithmetic carefully as calculator slips are common.

callouts.p: Show your working clearly by listing reactant bond calculations separately from product bond calculations to pick up error-carried-forward marks.

core.p: Similarly, list all bonds formed in the products, multiply their quantities by the given bond energy values, and sum them up. This gives the total energy released when new bonds are formed.
bullets: Tally all product bonds, quantities, and energies.
Sum the subtotals to find total energy released by forming bonds.
Remember that bond formation is inherently exothermic (releasing energy).
Keep the product sum distinct before performing the final subtraction step.

callouts.p: The total enthalpy decrease associated with the creation of stable attractive forces between nuclei and shared electron pairs in products.

core.h: Step 5: Final Subtraction and Sign Assignment
core.p: The final step applies the equation Delta H = (Energy to break bonds) - (Energy released forming bonds). It is critical to get the order of subtraction right. A positive final answer indicates an endothermic reaction, while a negative final answer indicates an exothermic reaction.
bullets: Subtract total product energy from total reactant energy.
Include units in your final answer (kJ/mol).
Explicitly include the positive (+) or negative (-) sign in your final answer.
Check if your calculated sign matches your qualitative understanding of the reaction type.

callouts.p: Subtracting reactants from products (Products - Reactants) is the exact reverse of thermodynamics convention and will result in the wrong mathematical sign for Delta H.

core.p: Consider the combustion of hydrogen gas to form water: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O. Using average bond energies (H-H = 436 kJ/mol, O=O = 498 kJ/mol, O-H = 464 kJ/mol), we can calculate the exact enthalpy change for this powerful reaction.
bullets: Reactant bonds broken: 2 x (H-H) and 1 x (O=O).
Reactant energy = (2 x 436) + (1 x 498) = 872 + 498 = 1370 kJ/mol.
Product bonds formed: 4 x (O-H) in two water molecules.
Product energy = 4 x 464 = 1856 kJ/mol.
Delta H = 1370 - 1856 = -486 kJ/mol (Exothermic).

callouts.p: All combustion reactions are exothermic, so their calculated Delta H must always be negative.

core.h: Why Bond Energies are Only Estimates
core.p: Bond energy values found in data books are average values derived from a wide range of different chemical compounds containing those bonds. For example, a C-H bond in methane has a slightly different bond energy than a C-H bond in ethanol because neighboring atoms influence electron density and bond strength.
bullets: Values are mean (average) bond enthalpies across many different molecules.
Actual bond energy depends on the molecular environment and neighboring atoms.
Calculations using bond energies are therefore approximations, not exact experimental measurements.
Calorimetry experiments yield experimental enthalpy changes that may differ slightly from bond energy calculations.

callouts.p: If an exam question asks why a calculated enthalpy change differs from a measured one, state clearly that bond energies are average values.

analogy.t: The Mortgage and House Purchase Analogy
analogy.p: Imagine buying and selling properties as a chemical reaction. Breaking bonds is like paying off an existing mortgage and selling your old house—it requires a massive upfront input of cash and effort (endothermic). Forming new bonds is like buying your dream home and receiving mortgage funds or moving in—it releases cash and stability into your life (exothermic). If you get more cash from your new setup than you spent breaking down the old one, you are in profit (exothermic reaction with a negative delta H). This breaks down because chemical bonds do not 'profit' in wealth, but it accurately maps the energetic ledger of input versus output.

terms.d: The energy required to break one mole of a specific covalent bond in gaseous molecules, measured in kJ/mol.
A reaction or process that absorbs energy from the surroundings, resulting in a temperature drop and a positive enthalpy change.
A reaction or process that releases energy into the surroundings, resulting in a temperature rise and a negative enthalpy change.
The heat energy change measured under constant pressure, represented by the symbol Delta H.
The mean energy needed to break a particular type of covalent bond, averaged across a range of different compounds.
A chemical formula that shows all the atoms and every covalent bond connecting them within a molecule.
The starting substances in a chemical reaction that undergo bond breaking.
The new substances formed in a chemical reaction resulting from bond formation.
The ratio of molecules of each reactant and product in a balanced chemical equation.
A chemical bond formed by the sharing of one or more pairs of electrons between two non-metal atoms.
The minimum amount of energy particles must have to collide successfully and start a reaction.
An experimental technique used to measure the amount of heat energy released or absorbed during a chemical reaction.

mistakes.w: Subtracting reactants from products backwards (Products minus Reactants).
mistakes.r: Always calculate Reactants minus Products (Energy to break minus Energy released).

mistakes.w: Forgetting to multiply bond energies by balancing numbers from the equation.
mistakes.r: Always check the coefficient in front of each molecule and multiply every bond in that molecule accordingly.

mistakes.w: Stating that bond formation is endothermic because it feels unnatural.
mistakes.r: Bond formation is always exothermic (releases energy) because atoms achieve a lower, more stable energy state.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to include the positive (+) or negative (-) sign in the final enthalpy change answer.
mistakes.r: Always include the sign; an exothermic value must have a minus sign.

mistakes.w: Treating diatomic oxygen (O2) as two single bonds instead of one double bond.
mistakes.r: Draw displayed formulas carefully: O2 has a double bond (O=O).

mistakes.w: Confusing bond energy with activation energy.
mistakes.r: Bond energy is the strength of a specific bond; activation energy is the total energy barrier for a reaction.

mistakes.w: Leaving units off the final calculated enthalpy change.
mistakes.r: Always include kJ/mol as the unit for enthalpy change calculations.

exam.q: Explain why bond breaking is an endothermic process.
model: Energy must be supplied/absorbed from the surroundings
To overcome the electrostatic forces of attraction between nuclei and shared electrons
exam.tip: Mention both energy absorption and overcoming attractive forces for full marks.

exam.q: Calculate the enthalpy change for the reaction H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl, given bond energies: H-H = 436 kJ/mol, Cl-Cl = 242 kJ/mol, H-Cl = 431 kJ/mol.
model: Energy in (bonds broken) = 436 + 242 = 678 kJ/mol
Energy out (bonds formed) = 2 x 431 = 862 kJ/mol
Delta H = 678 - 862
Delta H = -184 kJ/mol
exam.tip: Show your working clearly for energy in and energy out before subtracting.

exam.q: Explain why values obtained from bond energy calculations often differ slightly from experimental calorimetry results.
model: Bond energies used in calculations are average/mean values
Derived from a range of different compounds, not the specific molecule's exact environment
exam.tip: Use the key term 'average bond energy' to secure credit.

exam.q: State whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic if the energy released by forming bonds is greater than the energy absorbed breaking bonds.
model: Exothermic
exam.tip: Keep one-word answers precise when asked to state.

exam.q: Calculate the enthalpy change for the combustion of methane: CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O. Bond energies (kJ/mol): C-H = 413, O=O = 498, C=O = 805, O-H = 464.
model: Reactant bonds broken: (4 x 413) + (2 x 498) = 1652 + 996 = 2648 kJ/mol
Product bonds formed: (2 x 805) + (4 x 464) = 1610 + 1856 = 3466 kJ/mol
Delta H = -818 kJ/mol
Correct negative sign included
exam.tip: Check that methane has 4 C-H bonds and carbon dioxide has 2 C=O double bonds.

exam.q: Explain in terms of bond breaking and bond formation why a reaction is exothermic.
model: More energy is released when new bonds are formed
Than is absorbed to break existing bonds
exam.tip: Compare the two quantities directly rather than just defining them.

exam.q: What unit is used for enthalpy changes in bond energy calculations?
model: kJ/mol (kilojoules per mole)
exam.tip: Write kJ/mol clearly with correct capitalization.

exam.q: In a calculation, a student finds Delta H is +125 kJ/mol. Is this reaction exothermic or endothermic?
model: Endothermic
exam.tip: Positive sign always indicates endothermic.

exam.q: Describe how to use a displayed formula to count bonds in a reactant molecule.
model: Count every line representing a covalent bond between atoms
Multiply by the balancing coefficient of that molecule
exam.tip: Mention both counting individual bonds and multiplying by coefficients.

worked.q: Calculate the energy change for the reaction: N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3. Bond energies: N identical to N = 945 kJ/mol, H-H = 436 kJ/mol, N-H = 391 kJ/mol.
steps: Step 1: Identify and count bonds broken in reactants. 1 x (N identical to N) and 3 x (H-H).
Step 2: Calculate energy required to break bonds = (1 x 945) + (3 x 436) = 945 + 1308 = 2253 kJ/mol.
Step 3: Identify and count bonds formed in products. 2 molecules of NH3 each have 3 N-H bonds, so 6 x (N-H) in total.
Step 4: Calculate energy released forming bonds = 6 x 391 = 2346 kJ/mol.
Step 5: Calculate Delta H = Energy in - Energy out = 2253 - 2346 = -93 kJ/mol.

worked.q: Calculate the enthalpy change for the reaction: C2H4 + H2 -> C2H6. Bond energies: C=C = 612, C-C = 348, C-H = 413, H-H = 436 (all in kJ/mol).
steps: Step 1: Count bonds in reactants: 1 x (C=C), 4 x (C-H), 1 x (H-H).
Step 2: Calculate reactant energy = (1 x 612) + (4 x 413) + (1 x 436) = 612 + 1652 + 436 = 2700 kJ/mol.
Step 3: Count bonds in products (C2H6): 1 x (C-C), 6 x (C-H).
Step 4: Calculate product energy = (1 x 348) + (6 x 413) = 348 + 2478 = 2826 kJ/mol.
Step 5: Calculate Delta H = 2700 - 2826 = -126 kJ/mol.

chem_ocra.6.1.summary: Reaction profiles are graphical representations that show the relative energy levels of reactants and products during a chemical reaction, including the crucial role of activation energy. An exothermic reaction profile displays products at a lower energy level than reactants, whereas an endothermic profile displays products at a higher energy level. Understanding these diagrams allows chemists to visualise energy pathways, trace the energy barrier that must be overcome for a reaction to start, and evaluate how catalysts alter reaction mechanics.

core.p: A reaction profile is a line graph that charts how the overall chemical potential energy of a reacting system changes as the reaction progresses from start to finish. The horizontal axis represents the progress of the reaction (sometimes called reaction coordinate or time), while the vertical axis represents the potential energy of the particles involved. These graphs give instant visual proof of whether an overall energy change is releasing heat to the surroundings or absorbing it from them.
bullets: Horizontal axis shows the progress of the reaction from reactants to products.
Vertical axis shows the potential energy of the chemical system.
Reactants are always placed on the left-hand side of the profile.
Products are always placed on the right-hand side of the profile.

callouts.p: A graph that shows the relative energies of reactants and products, the activation energy, and the overall energy change of a chemical reaction.

fig.cap: A basic exothermic reaction profile showing reactants on the left, products on the lower right, and a peak in between representing the energy barrier.

core.p: Before any chemical reaction can begin, the reacting particles must collide with enough energy to break existing chemical bonds. The minimum amount of energy that particles must have to react successfully is known as the activation energy. On a reaction profile, this is visualised as the height of the energy hill between the reactants and the top of the curve. Reactions with very high activation energy barriers require a significant input of energy or a catalyst to proceed at a noticeable rate.
bullets: Symbolised by the term Ea in chemical equations and diagrams.
Measured as the energy difference between the reactants and the peak of the curve.
Represents the energy needed to break initial bonds in the reactants.
Higher activation energy means fewer particles have sufficient energy to react at room temperature.

callouts.p: The minimum amount of energy required for particles to collide with each other and react successfully.
On a profile, Ea is measured vertically from the energy level of the reactants up to the highest point (peak) of the curve.

core.p: In an exothermic reaction, energy is released to the surroundings, meaning the chemical energy stored within the bonds decreases. When drawing an exothermic reaction profile, the energy level of the products is lower than the energy level of the reactants. The overall energy change (Delta H) is negative. Despite releasing energy overall, the reaction still requires an initial input of activation energy to climb the energy barrier before the downhill drop to the products can occur.
bullets: Reactants start at a higher energy level than products.
The overall energy change (Delta H) is negative.
Energy is released to the surroundings, causing temperature to rise.
The peak is higher than the reactants, showing the activation energy barrier.

callouts.p: Students often think exothermic reactions need no energy to start. They always need activation energy to break initial bonds.

fig.cap: Detailed exothermic profile highlighting the activation energy and the negative overall energy change.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/><line x1="50" y1="200" x2="350" y2="200" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="30" x2="50" y2="200" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M 70 80 L 140 80 Q 200 10 260 80 L 330 160" fill="none" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="3"/><text x="70" y="70" font-size="11" fill="#1b2540">Reactants</text><text x="330" y="175" font-size="11" fill="#1b2540">Products</text><line x1="200" y1="10" x2="200" y2="80" stroke="#64748b" stroke-dasharray="4"/><text x="210" y="50" font-size="11" fill="#dc2626">Ea</text><line x1="70" y1="80" x2="200" y2="80" stroke="#64748b" stroke-dasharray="4"/><line x1="260" y1="160" x2="340" y2="160" stroke="#64748b" stroke-dasharray="4"/><text x="205" y="130" font-size="11" fill="#2563eb">Delta H (-)</text></svg>

core.p: In an endothermic reaction, energy is taken in from the surroundings, meaning the chemical energy stored within the bonds increases. On an endothermic reaction profile, the energy level of the products is higher than the energy level of the reactants. The overall energy change (Delta H) is positive. The activation energy in an endothermic reaction spans from the reactant line all the way up to the peak, and because products sit higher than reactants, the activation energy is often very large.
bullets: Reactants start at a lower energy level than products.
The overall energy change (Delta H) is positive.
Energy is absorbed from the surroundings, causing temperature to fall.
The energy required to break bonds is greater than the energy released when new bonds form.

callouts.p: Products are positioned vertically higher than reactants because thermal energy from the surroundings has been converted into chemical potential energy.

fig.cap: Endothermic reaction profile showing products higher than reactants and a positive overall energy change.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/><line x1="50" y1="200" x2="350" y2="200" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="30" x2="50" y2="200" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M 70 160 L 140 160 Q 200 60 260 160 L 330 90" fill="none" stroke="#0284c7" stroke-width="3"/><text x="70" y="175" font-size="11" fill="#1b2540">Reactants</text><text x="330" y="85" font-size="11" fill="#1b2540">Products</text><line x1="200" y1="60" x2="200" y2="160" stroke="#64748b" stroke-dasharray="4"/><text x="210" y="115" font-size="11" fill="#0284c7">Ea</text><line x1="70" y1="160" x2="200" y2="160" stroke="#64748b" stroke-dasharray="4"/><line x1="330" y1="90" x2="350" y2="90" stroke="#64748b" stroke-dasharray="4"/><text x="205" y="130" font-size="11" fill="#dc2626">Delta H (+)</text></svg>

core.p: The overall energy change of a reaction is represented by the symbol Delta H (enthalpy change). On a reaction profile, Delta H is measured as the vertical distance between the energy level of the reactants and the energy level of the products. If the products are lower than the reactants, Delta H is negative (exothermic). If the products are higher than the reactants, Delta H is positive (endothermic). The magnitude of Delta H tells us exactly how much energy is transferred per mole of reaction.
bullets: Delta H is negative for exothermic reactions.
Delta H is positive for endothermic reactions.
Calculated as Energy of Products minus Energy of Reactants.
Independent of the pathway taken or the activation energy barrier height.

callouts.p: Delta H = Energy(Products) - Energy(Reactants)

core.h: Effect of Catalysts on Reaction Profiles
core.p: A catalyst is a substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction without being chemically changed or used up by the end of the reaction. It works by providing an alternative reaction pathway that has a lower activation energy. On a reaction profile, the uncatalyzed pathway has a tall energy peak, while the catalyzed pathway is shown as a second curve with a lower peak. Because the activation energy is reduced, more colliding particles have enough energy to react, speeding up the reaction rate.
bullets: Catalysts lower the activation energy by providing an alternative pathway.
Represented on profiles by a lower peak drawn beneath the original curve.
Does not change the energy of the reactants or the products.
Does not change the overall energy change (Delta H).

callouts.p: When adding a catalyst curve to a profile, ensure the start and end points touch the original reactant and product lines precisely.

fig.cap: Reaction profile demonstrating how a catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy peak.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/><line x1="50" y1="200" x2="350" y2="200" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="30" x2="50" y2="200" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M 70 80 L 140 80 Q 200 10 260 80 L 330 160" fill="none" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M 70 80 Q 200 60 330 160" fill="none" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="3" stroke-dasharray="6"/><text x="70" y="70" font-size="11" fill="#1b2540">Reactants</text><text x="330" y="175" font-size="11" fill="#1b2540">Products</text><text x="210" y="35" font-size="10" fill="#dc2626">No Catalyst</text><text x="210" y="75" font-size="10" fill="#16a34a">With Catalyst</text></svg>

core.p: Exam questions frequently require students to distinguish between exothermic and endothermic profiles. The easiest way to identify them is to look at the relative positions of the reactant and product lines. In exothermic profiles, the product line is lower down the y-axis than the reactant line. In endothermic profiles, the product line is higher up the y-axis than the reactant line. Both profiles, however, feature an activation energy peak pointing upward from the reactants.
bullets: Exothermic: Products lower than reactants, Delta H negative.
Endothermic: Products higher than reactants, Delta H positive.
Both profiles require an activation energy peak starting from the reactant level.
Neither profile's overall Delta H is altered by adding a catalyst.

core.h: Bond Breaking and Bond Forming Mechanics
core.p: The height of the activation energy peak and the overall enthalpy change are governed by what happens to chemical bonds during a reaction. Breaking chemical bonds requires an input of energy, which is why energy must be absorbed to climb up to the peak of the reaction profile. Making new chemical bonds releases energy, which corresponds to the downward slope from the peak to the products. If more energy is released making bonds than was absorbed breaking them, the overall process is exothermic.
bullets: Bond breaking is always endothermic (absorbs energy, goes up).
Bond making is always exothermic (releases energy, goes down).
Peak height reflects the energy needed to break initial bonds.
Net energy change determines the final product position.

callouts.p: BARF: Breaking Absorbs, Releases Forms.

core.p: In higher-tier calculations and structured exam questions, you may be given a reaction profile with numerical values on the y-axis in kilojoules per mole (kJ/mol). To find the activation energy without a catalyst, subtract the reactant energy value from the peak energy value. To find the activation energy with a catalyst, subtract the reactant energy value from the catalyzed peak value. To find Delta H, subtract the reactant energy value from the product energy value.
bullets: Ea (uncatalyzed) = Peak Energy - Reactant Energy.
Ea (catalyzed) = Catalyzed Peak Energy - Reactant Energy.
Delta H = Product Energy - Reactant Energy.
Always check units given on the y-axis (typically kJ/mol).

core.p: When asked to sketch a reaction profile in an exam, precision and clear labelling are vital. You must always label both axes with 'Progress of reaction' and 'Potential energy'. Clear horizontal lines must be drawn for reactants and products, labelled explicitly. The curve must rise to a distinct peak representing activation energy. If comparing catalyzed and uncatalyzed reactions on the same axes, draw the catalyzed peak visibly lower than the original peak.
bullets: Always label both axes fully with quantities.
Use a ruler for axis lines and ensure arrows point in the correct directions.
Ensure reactant and product energy levels are distinctly different and labelled.
Check whether the question specifies exothermic or endothermic before drawing.

callouts.p: Examiners award zero marks for the curve if the axes are left unlabelled or incorrectly labelled.

analogy.p: Imagine you are hiking from a valley on the west side of a mountain range to a valley on the east side. The west valley represents your reactants, and the east valley represents your products. To get from one valley to the other, you cannot walk straight across; you must climb up and over the mountain pass. The height of that mountain pass from your starting valley is the activation energy -- the effort needed to get over the ridge. If the east valley is lower down than the west valley, you have finished at a lower altitude overall (exothermic). Where the analogy breaks down is that chemical reactions do not choose to climb passes out of willpower; particles rely on random kinetic collisions to scramble up the energy hill.

terms.d: A graph showing the potential energy of reactants and products during a chemical reaction.
The minimum amount of energy particles must collide with to react.
A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings, resulting in a temperature increase.
A reaction that takes in energy from the surroundings, resulting in a temperature decrease.
The overall change in thermal or chemical potential energy during a reaction.
A substance that speeds up a reaction by providing an alternative pathway with lower activation energy.
The starting substances in a chemical reaction, shown on the left of a profile.
The new substances formed in a chemical reaction, shown on the right of a profile.
The horizontal axis of a profile representing the advancement of a reaction over time.
The vertical axis of a profile representing the chemical energy stored in bonds.
A different route for reactant particles to form products, characteristic of catalyzed reactions.
The highest point on a reaction profile curve representing the transition state or maximum energy barrier.

mistakes.w: Drawing products higher than reactants for an exothermic reaction.
mistakes.r: Exothermic reactions must show products lower than reactants because energy is released.

mistakes.w: Measuring activation energy from the bottom of the graph axis.
mistakes.r: Activation energy is measured vertically from the reactant energy line up to the peak.

mistakes.w: Stating that a catalyst changes the overall Delta H value.
mistakes.r: A catalyst lowers the activation energy peak but leaves the reactant and product energy levels unchanged.

mistakes.w: Saying exothermic reactions have zero activation energy.
mistakes.r: All reactions require activation energy to break initial bonds, regardless of whether they are exothermic or endothermic.

mistakes.w: Labelling the y-axis simply as 'Energy' or 'Time'.
mistakes.r: The OCR mark scheme requires 'Potential energy' for the y-axis and 'Progress of reaction' for the x-axis.

mistakes.w: Drawing the catalyzed curve starting at a lower energy level than reactants.
mistakes.r: A catalyst does not alter the starting energy of the reactants; the curve must start on the reactant line.

exam.q: What is meant by the term 'activation energy'?
model: The minimum amount of energy required for particles to react
exam.tip: Learn this definition word for word as mark schemes are strict.

exam.q: Explain how a reaction profile shows whether a reaction is exothermic.
model: The energy of the products is lower than the energy of the reactants
Showing that energy is released overall
exam.tip: Reference both product and reactant relative positions.

exam.q: A reaction profile has reactants at 50 kJ/mol, a peak at 120 kJ/mol, and products at 20 kJ/mol. Calculate the activation energy.
model: = 70 kJ/mol
exam.tip: Subtract the reactant energy from the peak energy.

exam.q: Explain how a catalyst increases the rate of a chemical reaction using ideas about activation energy.
model: Provides an alternative pathway
Which has a lower activation energy
So more particles have energy greater than or equal to the activation energy and collide successfully
exam.tip: Include all three standard marking points for catalyst questions.

exam.q: Sketch a labelled reaction profile for an endothermic reaction.
model: Correctly labelled axes (Potential energy and Progress of reaction)
Reactants lower than products
A curve showing an activation energy peak
exam.tip: Use a ruler for axes and make sure the product line is visibly higher than the reactant line.

exam.q: Using the profile data from question 3, calculate the overall energy change (Delta H).
model: = -30 kJ/mol
exam.tip: Delta H is Products minus Reactants. Remember the negative sign for exothermic.

exam.q: Explain why adding a catalyst does not change the overall energy change of a reaction.
model: It lowers the activation energy by providing an alternative pathway
The starting energy of reactants and final energy of products remain unchanged
exam.tip: Mention that reactant and product levels stay identical.

exam.q: State what the peak of a reaction profile represents.
model: The activation energy or transition state
exam.tip: Keep the answer concise and direct.

exam.q: Describe the energy change that occurs during bond breaking.
model: Energy is absorbed (endothermic)
exam.tip: Remember BARF: Breaking Absorbs.

exam.q: Compare the activation energy of an uncatalyzed reaction with that of a catalyzed reaction on a reaction profile.
model: The catalyzed reaction has a lower peak than the uncatalyzed reaction
Showing that less energy is required for the reaction to take place
exam.tip: Contrast the heights of the two peaks clearly.

worked.q: For a chemical reaction, the energy of the reactants is 150 kJ/mol, the peak of the uncatalyzed reaction profile is 280 kJ/mol, and the energy of the products is 90 kJ/mol. A catalyst is added which reduces the peak height to 210 kJ/mol. Calculate: (a) The activation energy without a catalyst, (b) The activation energy with a catalyst, (c) The overall energy change (Delta H).
steps: For uncatalyzed activation energy: subtract reactant energy from uncatalyzed peak energy. Ea = 280 - 150.
For catalyzed activation energy: subtract reactant energy from catalyzed peak energy. Ea (catalyzed) = 210 - 150.
For overall energy change (Delta H): subtract reactant energy from product energy. Delta H = 90 - 150.

worked.q: An endothermic reaction has reactants at 200 kJ/mol and products at 350 kJ/mol. The activation energy is 180 kJ/mol. Calculate the energy at the peak of the reaction profile and the overall Delta H.
steps: To find peak energy, add the activation energy to the reactant energy. Peak = 200 + 180 = 380 kJ/mol.
To find Delta H, subtract reactant energy from product energy. Delta H = 350 - 200 = +150 kJ/mol.
worked.ans: Peak energy is 380 kJ/mol, Delta H is +150 kJ/mol.
